content: A history of epigastric pain, loss of appetite, and weight loss is indicative of peptic ulcer disease. The most common symptoms of peptic ulcer disease include: Epigastric pain: In cases of gastric ulcers, the pain typically worsens with food intake, whereas in duodenal ulcers, the pain tends to improve after eating. Indigestion (dyspepsia). Nausea and vomiting. Hematemesis, which refers to the presence of blood in vomitus. The presence of blood in stools, which may indicate gastrointestinal bleeding. Loss of appetite. Unintentional weight loss. When documenting a patient’s history, it is essential to focus on key components such as: Past medical history, including any previous diagnoses or treatments for gastrointestinal conditions. Family history, particularly of gastrointestinal diseases or conditions that may predispose the patient to peptic ulcer disease. Social history, including occupational factors, alcohol consumption (with details on quantity and frequency), smoking habits, and any history of drug use. Allergies, especially to medications that may be relevant to treatment. It is important to note that this section should not describe the natural progression of the disease or provide a historical perspective on its discovery or management. Less common symptoms of peptic ulcer disease may also be documented, though they are not as frequently observed in patients.
